posts.topic: AGI and interest rates — why transformative AI could suppress rather than raise the cost of capital
posts.source_headline: AGI Could Lower Interest Rates
posts.x_post: The standard macro assumption about AGI gets the direction of interest rates exactly backwards. Every economist running a standard growth model concludes that expectations of transformative AI should push long-term rates higher — faster growth means more competition for capital, higher returns, higher discount rates. A new heterogeneous-agent asset pricing model shows the opposite can hold, and the mechanism matters enormously for how to price assets over the next decade. The key variable is wealth concentration. When AGI automates most human labor, the gains flow overwhelmingly to capital owners. Capital owners, almost by definition, have a much lower marginal propensity to consume than workers do. That surplus savings floods into financial markets rather than into goods markets. Aggregate demand for capital investment rises, but the supply of savings rises faster. The result: the real rate of return falls even as economic output accelerates sharply. This mirrors what happened during the early stages of the original Industrial Revolution, when productivity surged in specific sectors while the broader population experienced falling real wages, and bond yields in Britain compressed rather than exploded. The second-order consequence crushes the standard narrative that AI will force central banks into a tightening cycle. If AGI lands as a deflationary supply shock concentrated in the hands of asset owners, the Fed faces structurally low neutral rates, not a return to the 1970s. Duration assets and fixed income outperform in that world; commodity-linked inflation hedges underperform. Positioning for AGI as an inflationary event is the consensus trade. It may also be the wrong one.

Brian Chesky himself called out that there is no consumer business model for AI he has seen that scales past a local maximum. The second-order consequence is a talent concentration effect. The 16 consumer-focused companies in that batch will recruit from the same pool as the 159 enterprise ones, at lower expected revenue multiples. That means consumer AI as a category runs lean or runs out of runway before it finds distribution. The parallel to 2012 mobile is instructive. Enterprise dominated early SaaS on mobile too, until one consumer behavior, photo sharing, unlocked a new monetization surface. The category that unlocks consumer AI monetization has not shipped yet. Until it does, every YC batch will look like this one.

posts.topic: Buffett Indicator at 215% and what Buffett's own cash position reveals about the signal
posts.source_headline:
The Buffett Indicator just crossed 215%. The 2000 dot-com peak was 137%. The 2007 housing peak was 105%.

The man the metric is named after parked $397 billion
posts.x_post:
The Buffett Indicator has become the most famous metric its namesake refuses to act on, which tells you everything about how markets actually work right now.

The ratio crossed 215% this week. The dot-com peak in 2000 hit 137%. The 2007 housing bubble peak hit 105%. Both preceded collapses of 49% and 57% in the S&P 500 respectively. By any historical calibration, 215% should be a five-alarm warning.

Buffett parked $347 billion in Treasury bills at Berkshire by end of 2024. That number grew from $168 billion in 2023, meaning he doubled his cash position in 12 months while the market ran hard. He also sold $134 billion in equities net during that same period, cutting Apple by roughly 67% from peak holdings. The man is not buying what the indicator describes.

Here is the mechanism worth understanding. The Buffett Indicator assumes GDP is the economy's productive floor, the base against which equity prices should be measured. But $7.6 trillion in passive index flows since 2010 means price discovery runs on momentum as much as earnings. Passive funds buy proportionally regardless of valuation. That structural bid keeps the ratio elevated without the speculative mania that preceded prior crashes.

The second-order consequence is that a high ratio alone predicts neither timing nor magnitude. Japan's equivalent stayed above 100% for two decades post-1989 and still compounded returns for patient holders of certain sectors. The US has structurally higher corporate profit margins than any prior comparable period, averaging 12.4% net margin for S&P 500 companies versus 6.1% in 2000.

The indicator flags a genuine risk. Buffett's cash pile is the hedge against it. The signal to watch is the gap between those two numbers closing.

posts.topic: AI chatbot legal liability and corporate accountability
posts.source_headline: Jake Moffatt's grandmother died in November 2022. He went online to book a flight to her funeral. Air Canada's chatbot told him there was a bereavement fare pro
posts.x_post:
The Air Canada chatbot case is the most important AI liability ruling most people filed under 'funny customer service story.' A British Columbia tribunal ruled in 2024 that Air Canada bore full responsibility for misinformation its chatbot gave Jake Moffatt about bereavement fares. Moffatt paid for a bereavement flight, the chatbot told him to apply for the discount within 90 days after travel, the real policy required application before departure. Air Canada lost and owed Moffatt $812.02 CAD plus fees.

The mechanism matters more than the outcome. Air Canada argued the chatbot was a 'separate legal entity' responsible for its own statements. The tribunal rejected that outright. A company deploying an automated system inherits every representation that system makes, regardless of whether a human reviewed it. The chatbot's error rate is irrelevant. The deployment decision is the liability trigger.

Now stack that principle against the current AI deployment wave. Enterprises are pushing customer-facing agents across insurance claims, loan applications, medical triage, and travel bookings. Every one of those agents will occasionally hallucinate a policy, misquote a rate, or invert a deadline, just as the Air Canada bot inverted Moffatt's. The legal exposure scales with deployment surface, and most legal teams have not caught up to that math. A $812 judgment becomes a class action the moment 4,000 users receive the same wrong instruction.

The Moffatt ruling redraws where accountability sits in the AI stack. The model vendor does not absorb it. The integration partner does not absorb it. The enterprise that deployed the agent absorbs it, fully, on the first wrong answer. Boards approving AI rollout plans in 2025 are approving liability schedules they have not yet priced.
posts.substack_note:
Most people heard the Air Canada chatbot story as a quirky consumer-rights win. I keep reading it as the liability template that enterprise legal teams have not yet internalized.

Here is what actually happened. Jake Moffatt asked Air Canada's chatbot about bereavement fares in late 2022. The bot told him to buy the ticket and apply for the discount within 90 days after travel. The real policy required application before departure. Air Canada lost in tribunal and had to pay $812.02 CAD plus fees.

The part that should keep enterprise CIOs up at night: Air Canada argued its chatbot was a 'separate legal entity' that bore its own responsibility for its statements. The tribunal dismissed that in a single paragraph. Deploy the agent, own its outputs. Full stop.

That principle, applied at scale, changes the economics of customer-facing AI dramatically. A hallucinated policy instruction costs $812 when one customer catches it. It costs seven figures when the same instruction goes to thousands of users before anyone notices. The deployment decision is the liability trigger, and the error rate of the underlying model does not factor into the legal analysis at all.

Boards are approving AI deployment roadmaps right now. Very few of those approvals include a line item for what happens when the agent gets a policy backwards. The Moffatt case says that line item is mandatory.

posts.topic: Anthropic named AI agents as a B2B sales strategy — shifting budget ownership from IT to finance
posts.source_headline:
Anthropic just gave each of these five agents a name. "GL Reconciler." "KYC Screener." "Valuation Reviewer." "Month-End Closer." "Statement Auditor."

That nami
posts.x_post:
Anthropic just solved the most expensive problem in enterprise software sales, and it had nothing to do with the model. Naming five finance agents — GL Reconciler, KYC Screener, Valuation Reviewer, Month-End Closer, Statement Auditor — moved Anthropic out of IT procurement and into finance team budgets, where the average Fortune 500 controller owns $8–14 million in recurring vendor spend and signs checks without a CTO's approval. That single naming decision changed the buyer, the budget line, and the competitive set simultaneously.

Enterprise AI has been stuck because CIOs buy capability and hold it in a cost center. Finance leaders buy outcomes and charge them to the function. A line item called "Month-End Closer at $X per close" maps directly onto the $180,000–$240,000 fully loaded annual cost of the controller it shadows. That comparison closes itself. A line item called "Claude Sonnet 4.6 with finance prompts" competes against Okta and endpoint security tools in an IT budget that is already squeezed.

Each named agent also carries an implicit SLA. Naming something a "KYC Screener" means Anthropic accepts accountability for KYC outcomes, which forces them to build compliance audit trails, explainability logs, and exception workflows they would have happily skipped if the product was just an API. The name creates the product spec, then the compliance requirements, then the reference customer story.

The deeper pattern: the companies that won in prior enterprise software waves — Workday, ServiceNow, Veeva — all did this. They took horizontal database or workflow technology and wrapped named, role-specific products around it so that the buyer was a business unit head, never a platform architect.

Anthropic just ran the same playbook. The five names are not marketing. They are org chart entries, and org chart entries get defended in budget cuts.
posts.substack_note:

The average Fortune 500 controller owns $8–14 million in recurring vendor spend and can approve a named software product without CTO sign-off.

"Month-End Closer at $X per close" is a finance team line item. "Claude Sonnet 4.6 with finance prompts" is an IT line item. That difference determines whether the product survives its first renewal cycle.

That forces Anthropic to build audit logs, exception handling, and compliance trails they would have skipped as a general-purpose API vendor. The name generates the product spec.

Workday, ServiceNow, and Veeva all ran this same playbook — wrap horizontal technology in named, role-specific products so business unit heads own the budget. Anthropic just did it in one announcement.

The five names are not branding. They are org chart insertions, and org chart insertions are the hardest thing to remove in an enterprise.

For a decade, the crypto narrative was that Western Union's fee structure and physical network were relics waiting to be disrupted. I never fully bought that. Physical presence in 200 countries is not a bug. It is the moat. The question was always whether Western Union would use it first.

They are. The legacy rails and the new rails are converging, and the winner so far looks like whoever holds both simultaneously. What does this mean for pure-play stablecoin remittance startups who bet on WU's slow death?

For two months, Iran hit UAE infrastructure with 438 ballistic missiles, 2,012 drones, and 19 cruise missiles while both sat inside the same cartel quota framework. Membership was costing Abu Dhabi roughly 1.4 million barrels per day in suppressed output.

Four years after Libra collapsed under regulatory pressure, Meta didn't launch a new coin. The question I keep returning to: does Meta expand this to advertising disbursements? If brand payments follow creator payments, you have a stablecoin network processing commercial-scale volumes before most analysts notice.

posts.topic: UAE captures 66% of MENA's contracting Q1 2026 funding
posts.source_headline: MENA startup funding slips to $941 million in Q1 2026 amid heightened geopolitical risk
posts.x_post: MENA startup funding collapsed 37% year-on-year in Q1 2026 to $941 million, but the real number is UAE's capture rate: $625.8 million of that, 66% of the entire region, across just 46 deals. Saudi Arabia pulled in $156.7 million across 57 deals. My read: MENA's innovation capital is not slowing. It is concentrating. The Hormuz disruptions accelerated the flight to certainty, and UAE is where certainty lives.
posts.substack_note:
My read: when total MENA startup funding falls 37% year-on-year, the instinct is to call it a regional slowdown. The data says something more specific.

UAE raised $625.8 million in Q1 2026, capturing 66% of the region's entire $941 million. Saudi Arabia ran 57 deals but raised only $156.7 million. Egypt pulled in $86 million across 12 transactions.

I'm based in the UAE, and I've seen this pattern before: when regional risk spikes, capital doesn't leave MENA. It relocates within MENA. Iran's Hormuz blockade created genuine uncertainty across seaborne logistics. Investors still wanted regional exposure. They just wanted it from a jurisdiction with regulatory clarity and no proximity to the disruption.

Fintech led at 46% of total funding. That's what investors trust when nervous: clear revenue models, not speculative bets.

What does this concentration mean for founders building from Cairo or Riyadh? I'm still working through that.

posts.topic: World Bank moves Pakistan from South Asia into MENAAP
posts.source_headline: Pakistan's New Geographic Designation Brings Complications
posts.x_post: The World Bank just reclassified Pakistan from South Asia into MENAAP, a new regional group covering the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan. MENAAP now has 813 million people; Pakistan alone is nearly 300 million, one-third of the group. My read: this is not a bureaucratic update. When the institution that sets global development benchmarks moves Pakistan into the Gulf's orbit, every sovereign wealth fund, multilateral lender, and MSCI index will follow.
posts.substack_note:
My take: the World Bank's decision to move Pakistan into MENAAP looks like a data reorganization exercise. It isn't.

MENA's population jumps from 519 million to 813 million with Pakistan included. Pakistan now anchors the new grouping at nearly one-third of total MENAAP population. The young-age dependency ratio for the region rises by 15%, which changes every development model and sovereign lending thesis for the combined bloc.

I've watched Pakistan's economic center of gravity tilt toward the Gulf for years. GCC remittances, hundreds of thousands of Pakistani workers across UAE and Saudi Arabia, deepening trade ties. The World Bank just made it official in the language that multilaterals, index providers, and institutional investors actually use.

Once Bloomberg, MSCI, and the Asian Development Bank retag Pakistan, capital flows follow. Is Islamabad prepared to be benchmarked against MENA peers rather than South Asian ones?

My take: MENA startup funding fell to $941 million in Q1 2026, down 37% year-on-year and 21% quarter-on-quarter. The monthly collapse is the real story. February closed at $326.6 million as the Iran war intensified. March closed at just $48.3 million, against a 2025 annual record of $7.5 billion.

posts.topic: Meta relaunches stablecoin creator payments via USDC/Stripe

posts.x_post: Meta killed its own stablecoin project, Diem, in January 2022 rather than fight regulators for the right to issue currency. Four years later, the replacement uses USDC not Diem, Stripe not Novi, Polygon and Solana not a proprietary chain, and launches in Colombia and Philippines, two of the world's largest remittance corridors. My read: the $293 billion stablecoin market built itself in Meta's absence, and Meta just quietly re-entered as a distribution layer.
posts.substack_note: I keep thinking about how quietly Meta walked back into the stablecoin conversation. In January 2022, Diem was sold off and pronounced dead — a generational ambition to issue private currency, ended without a fight. Four years later, the same company is paying creators in USDC, on Polygon and Solana, through Stripe, in Colombia and the Philippines. The $293B stablecoin market grew without them, and now they are entering as plumbing, not as the protagonist. My read: this is what conceding the issuance war but winning the distribution war looks like. The interesting question is whether the next layer down — wallets, remittance UX, fiat off-ramps — is actually the higher-margin layer all along. Curious how others are reading this. Are we underestimating what 'distribution-only' fintech looks like at Meta scale?
